newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court rejects police drug search power.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court rejects police drug search power.

text.p: A unanimous Supreme Court Monday refused to exempt police on drug raids from the general requirement that they knock and announce their identity before searching for evidence.

The court, which ruled in 1995 that the knock-and-announce requirement governing police conduct must be scrutinised under constitutional standards, did not state that all police searches must be preceded by an announcement but said it depended on the circumstances of each case.

In a second police-related ruling, the high court by a 5-4 vote made it harder for local governments to be held liable for damages in civil cases alleging excessive force when a police officer has been hired despite past offences.

The court said an Oklahoma county cannot be held liable for a sheriff's isolated decision to hire an officer without proper screening. The hiring must involve the "conscious disregard" that the officer poses a high risk to use too much force.

In the search case, the justices disagreed with a Wisconsin Supreme Court ruling that allowed a blanket exception to the requirement when drugs are the object of the search warrant being executed by the police.

The nation's high court said the Constitution's Fourth Amendment, which bars unreasonable searches and seizures of evidence, does not permit an across-the-board exception for drug investigations from the knock-and-announce rule.
Wisconsin argued that drugs can be easily destroyed and drug dealers often are armed and dangerous, two factors it said justified giving the police a blanket exemption.

But Justice John Paul Stevens wrote for the high court that creating exceptions to the requirement presented serious concerns. He said they would impermissibly insulate from judicial review drug cases which do not pose special risks to officers and he warned that creating exceptions for categories of crimes would make the knock-and-announce rule meaningless.

Most states generally allow police to use force to enter a residence only after they announce their presence to carry out a search or to conduct an arrest. Stevens said a no-knock entry would be justified when the police had a reasonable suspicion that announcing their presence would be dangerous or would inhibit the investigation of the crime.

The case involved Steiney Richards, whose hotel room in Madison, Wisconsin, police entered without knocking at 3:40 a.m. on Dec. 31, 1991. Drugs were seized from the room but Richards, who was convicted and sentenced to 13 years in prison, sought to suppress them as an unconstitutional search.
The Supreme Court said the evidence in the case established that the decision by the police to enter the hotel room was reasonable under the circumstances.

The Oklahoma case involved Stacy Burns, who had been hired as a deputy sheriff in Bryan County despite a long record of assault, public drunkenness, driving while intoxicated and traffic violations. He was the sheriff's nephew.

A woman sued the county for damages, charging that Brown used excessive force during an unlawful arrest in 1991. She said the county should be held liable for the sheriff's hiring and training decisions.

But Justice Sandra Day O'Connor said for the court majority that Congress did not intend to impose liability on a city or county unless deliberate action attributable to it had been the key force behind the violation of federal rights.

"Cases involving constitutional injuries allegedly traceable to an ill-considered hiring decision pose the greatest risk that a municipality will be held liable for an injury that it did not cause," she said.
The high court's ruling overturned an award of more than $800,000 in damages and attorney fees against the county.
